 has moved to the center of healthcare conversations after filing its third-quarter earnings release with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The document shows a company whose top line was roughly unchanged from a year earlier, yet whose earnings from operations rose sharply as the medical care ratio improved and Optum businesses became more efficient. Management also lifted its full-year earnings per share guidance, reflecting results through the end of September. The stock is a long-standing component of the S&P 500, so any change in its guidance tends to be noticed well beyond managed care. The quarter matters because UnitedHealth Group spent much of the preceding period explaining elevated medical costs, shrinking membership and a broad operational reset. The new release reads like a progress report on that reset. It describes pricing and benefit changes in Medicare Advantage, tighter medical cost management, the planned exit of unprofitable Optum Health markets and a clear promise to simplify the experience of patients and clinicians. Market participants frequently monitor Healthcare Stocks to better understand trends affecting large insurers and care delivery groups, and this filing provides a detailed data point for that broader picture. The sections below walk through the release in plain language. They separate what the company reported as fact from what remains expectation, explain how each of its four main businesses fits together, and highlight the commitments on prior authorization, rebates and governance that accompanied the numbers. Nothing here is advice; the aim is to help readers follow the primary documents. The earnings release, furnished as an exhibit to a Form eight-K, describes revenue that was roughly flat to slightly lower than in the same quarter a year earlier. That is a notable statement for a company that normally grows its top line, and it is explained by deliberate choices: membership fell in several products, and Optum Health stepped back from markets where it did not have enough value-based care presence to run the model well. Despite the flat revenue, earnings from operations rose sharply and the net margin improved. Both generally accepted and adjusted earnings per share moved higher than in the prior-year quarter. Operating cash generation was strong relative to net earnings, which is the kind of conversion that long-term holders of insurer stock tend to watch because it indicates that reported earnings are turning into cash rather than sitting in receivables or reserves. The balance sheet commentary was measured. The ratio of debt to total capital edged up from the previous quarter, but the company reiterated its aim of reaching roughly two-fifths by the end of the year. It also continued to pay dividends and carry out its share capital program, which signals that management sees the financial position as stable enough to keep rewarding equity owners while it works the leverage ratio down. Readers should keep in mind that favorable development of prior-period medical reserves helped the quarter. Reserve releases are legitimate, but they are also a reminder that part of the improvement reflects estimates from earlier periods turning out better than expected, not purely new-quarter performance. The medical care ratio compares the money the insurer pays out for patient care with the premiums it collects. For a business whose premiums are largely fixed at the start of a plan year, a small move in that ratio can swing earnings dramatically. During the difficult stretch before this report, the ratio had worsened as utilization rose, especially among older members, and as certain outpatient and specialty services cost more than priced. In the third-quarter release the ratio improved year over year. Management credited cost management, benefit and pricing changes, and care delivery initiatives. In practical terms that means plan designs were adjusted for the current year, some unprofitable counties or products were trimmed, and the company pushed harder on coordination of care so that fewer patients reach expensive settings unnecessarily. The operating cost ratio also improved, although the release candidly states that the company is spending more on technology, artificial intelligence enabled operations and staff. That is a useful nuance. Efficiency gains are not coming only from cutting spending; some of the cost base is being redirected toward tools meant to speed up claims, documentation and payment accuracy. Because the ratio can be influenced by the mix of members, seasonality and the timing of reserve changes, it rarely tells a complete story in one quarter. Market participants therefore compare it across several periods, and they watch how management explains the contribution of reserve development versus underlying medical trend. UnitedHealthcare is the insurance operation that offers employer plans, Medicare Advantage, Medicare supplement and Part D, and Medicaid managed care. In the quarter its revenue declined slightly while earnings and margin rose. That combination is the signature of a business pruning less attractive membership and repricing what remains. Membership shrank in employer, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid categories. The release points to employer attrition and to changes in Medicaid eligibility as drivers, both of which are largely outside the insurer's direct control. Medicare and Retirement revenue fell because of membership and product mix, which fits the company's earlier decision to exit plans and regions where benefits could not be supported by the payments received from the federal program. An important dated reference point for the Medicare Advantage business is the quality rating system, commonly called Stars. Management said the results for the coming plan year were in line with expectations and showed improvement on many quality measures. Star ratings influence bonus payments and marketing advantages, so a result described as in line removes one unknown rather than adding a surprise. The competitive context includes other large insurers such as CVS Health through Aetna, Elevance Health, Humana and Cigna, all of which have been recalibrating Medicare Advantage offers. UnitedHealthcare is the largest participant, which makes its choices about benefits and county footprints influential for the whole industry. Optum Health is the care delivery arm, including primary care clinics, multispecialty groups, ambulatory surgery centers and value-based arrangements in which providers are paid for keeping a defined population healthy. Revenue there fell meaningfully in the quarter, and the release attributes this to exiting markets where the company lacked sufficient value-based care presence. At the same time, earnings in the unit rose sharply from a level near breakeven. Management linked the improvement to operational discipline and to better medical cost management. For a care delivery business that depends on paying clinicians and facilities while bearing some of the medical cost exposure, the move away from near-breakeven performance is a meaningful signal that the restructuring is starting to take effect. The logic of shrinking to improve is straightforward. Value-based care works best with density: enough patients in a region that clinicians can coordinate, share data and spread fixed costs. Where density is thin, the unit economics are harder, and a decision to exit can raise average performance even as revenue declines. Readers should treat the revenue decline as intentional and look at whether earnings per patient keep improving. The stakes are high because Optum Health is also tied to the Medicare Advantage strategy. When UnitedHealthcare membership changes, the number of patients flowing into Optum clinics changes too, so the two businesses must be managed together rather than as separate silos. Optum Insight supplies data, analytics, revenue cycle tools and technology services to hospitals, physician groups and health plans. Its revenue grew modestly in the quarter and earnings increased, which management tied to new product offerings and efficiencies. The release highlights artificial intelligence tools for clinical documentation and for payment accuracy, an area where automation could shorten the time between a patient visit and a properly adjudicated claim. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit business, saw revenue roughly flat while earnings rose. The release credits growth in biosimilar adoption and operational gains. Prescription volume declined, mainly because of membership losses in UnitedHealthcare, a reminder that the insurer and pharmacy businesses move together because many Optum Rx members arrive through the health plan. Pharmacy benefit managers have been under intense scrutiny from lawmakers, employers and state attorneys general over rebates, spread pricing and the opacity of net costs. Against that backdrop, the company said it is moving toward a fee-based, transparent pharmacy model. Competitors include Express Scripts from Cigna and Caremark from CVS Health, and all three have been pressed to adjust how they are paid. The combined message from Insight and Rx is that Optum is trying to be seen less as a collection of intermediaries and more as a set of technology and service tools whose value can be measured. Whether customers agree is something upcoming contract cycles will reveal. Alongside the financial statements, the release lists several commitments that respond to criticism from patients, physicians and policymakers. The most visible is a step to reduce prior authorization requirements. Management said that by the end of the year it intends to eliminate about three-tenths of prior approval volume. Prior authorization is the process in which a clinician must obtain insurer approval before certain services or drugs, and it has been blamed for delays in care and for administrative burden on physician offices. A second commitment concerns manufacturer drug rebates. The company pledged to pass through the full amount of rebates it receives to clients by a stated year later in the decade. It also said it is rebating earnings on individual plans offered under the Affordable Care Act for the current year. These are unusual statements for a large insurer, and they show the degree to which public pressure is shaping corporate behavior. A third commitment is financial and philanthropic: one billion dollars directed to the United Health Foundation, focused on rural, maternal, child and behavioral health. The pledge is large, though it is spread over time and is separate from operating results. None of these items is a certainty about how events will unfold; they are announced intentions. Their real impact will depend on how clinicians, employers and regulators experience the changes, and on whether the company can maintain medical cost discipline while making approvals easier. Chief executive Stephen Hemsley framed the quarter around discipline and execution. In the release he said the company aims to deliver a simpler, more supportive experience for patients and the clinicians who care for them. The emphasis on simplicity echoes the broader theme that a complicated structure, many overlapping programs and uneven execution contributed to the earlier troubles. The release also describes governance changes. The board created a Public Responsibility Committee, named a new lead independent director and added a new independent director. Committees of this type are meant to oversee issues such as patient access, public trust and societal impact, which have moved from the periphery to the center of the insurer's reputation. Governance changes are easy to announce and harder to evaluate. Market participants usually look for evidence in how often the new committee reports, how it interacts with management and whether the board is willing to challenge strategy. The addition of an independent lead director can provide a counterweight, particularly while the company is under regulatory and political scrutiny. For readers, the key point is that the quarter included not just numbers but also structural signals. Those signals reinforce management's argument that the reset is organizational as well as financial, though the final judgment rests on sustained performance. The first uncertainty is medical cost trend. Utilization among older members, the cost of specialty drugs and the pace of outpatient procedures all affect the medical care ratio. The improvement reported in the third quarter is welcome, but a single period does not settle whether the underlying trend has stabilized. The role of favorable reserve development in that improvement is another reason for caution. The second is membership. The release acknowledges decreases across employer, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid. Some of this is deliberate, but shrinking membership can reduce scale advantages in negotiating with providers and pharmacies. The upcoming annual enrollment period for Medicare Advantage will offer a fresh signal about how benefit changes are received. The third is regulation and public scrutiny. Federal agencies, congressional committees and state regulators continue to examine Medicare Advantage coding practices, pharmacy benefit management and prior authorization. Commitments made in the release may help the company's standing but cannot remove those inquiries. The fourth is execution of the Optum restructuring, particularly the balance between exiting markets and maintaining care continuity for patients. Each of these items is a matter of expectation rather than fact, and the company's own guidance language includes the usual caveat that results can differ from what management anticipates. Full-year guidance was raised, with generally accepted earnings per share expected to be at least a stated floor and adjusted earnings per share at least a somewhat higher floor. The wording matters: both are phrased as minimums, which leaves room for the final figure to be higher but also reflects that only one quarter remains. Because the figures reflect results through the third quarter, much of the full-year number is already locked in. What the release does not do is supply a detailed bridge for the final quarter. Readers cannot determine from the document alone how much of the remaining quarter is expected to come from underlying improvement and how much from the timing of reserves, portfolio gains or seasonal patterns. For a Medicare-heavy insurer, the fourth quarter often brings higher utilization as deductibles are met, so seasonality is a real factor. It is also worth remembering that guidance is a management statement of expectations. It is not a promise, and it is subject to the same medical cost, regulatory and economic variables that affected earlier quarters. Careful readers compare the language in the release with the more detailed discussion in the later quarterly filing and with remarks made on the conference call. The most reliable source is the earnings release itself, filed as an exhibit on the company's Form eight-K at the Securities and Exchange Commission. A companion supplemental document in the same filing presents the figures in a more tabular layout. The company also publishes an announcement of its earnings date through a wire service, which confirms the timing and the conference call details. Other helpful primary sources include the quarterly report on Form ten-Q, which carries detailed notes on reserves, legal matters and segment results, and the annual report, which describes the business model and the main uncertainties in depth. Exchange quote pages provide a convenient place to follow the company's trading symbol and corporate actions. Third-party commentary can be helpful for context, but readers should always compare it with these primary sources, because summaries can omit nuance or misstate details. This article states only what the published documents support and avoids numerical specifics so that nothing is misquoted. title: Meet UNH’s New AD, Ryan Colton - The New Hampshire
content: The stadium seats are filling, the student section is cheering, and the band's sound carries across the field on a crisp Saturday in Durham. As fans gather to watch the Wildcats take the field, a new face becomes a familiar presence in the stands: Ryan Colton, the University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) new athletic director. In July 2026, UNH’s President, Elizabeth Chilton, appointed Colton to lead the university’s 20-sport NCAA Division I athletic program. From Saturday football games to winter hockey games, Colton’s role extends far beyond the playing field, encompassing the student-athletes, campus community, and the fans who make up Wildcat athletics. Before arriving in Durham, Colton spent eight years at the University of Richmond in Virginia. His career in athletics administration also includes time at the College of the Holy Cross and Providence College. But his path to athletics leadership was not a conventional one. Colton studied political science at Bucknell University, where he also played quarterback for the football team. It was there that he developed a passion for intercollegiate athletics. After graduating, Colton attended New England Law in Boston and worked as a practicing attorney for several years before making the transition into athletics administration. “While I worked hard with long hours in both [Law and Athletic Administration], I really had a passion for intercollegiate athletics and the impact it can have on young people and the campus and broader community,” Colton said. “For me, this has really been a labor of love; I really do love coming to work every day.” Now, as he settles into his new role at UNH, Colton is focused on strengthening the connection between athletics and the broader university community. He wants student-athletes to be involved beyond their prospective teams and sees opportunities for athletics to bring students, faculty, and residents together. “I love working with colleagues across campus, whether it be in the president's office from deans to professors, on ways we can all collaborate to better support not just our student-athletes but also our students across campus,” Colton said. “I want to give a really great student-athlete experience, but also, how can our sports better improve the experience for all students across the board and the pride across the institution?” A central goal of Colton’s is the “whole-student athlete” experience. For him, supporting student-athletes means looking beyond their performance on the field or court. Academic achievement, personal growth, and a sense of belonging are also important parts of their college experience. Colton also hopes to strengthen the sense of community among UNH’s athletic program, encouraging teams to support one another and using sports as a way to build pride across the university and throughout New Hampshire. Balancing the needs of 20 different sports can be difficult, but Colton approaches the responsibility by focusing on the people behind each program. As he reflects on his belief that the value of college athletics extends beyond competition, he attends as many games as possible to show his support for student-athletes and coaches. The commitment has quickly become a family affair. Colton’s wife, Brittany, and their two children, Grady and Ella, have joined him in embracing their new Wildcat community. Ryan Colton and his wife Brittany, son Grady and daughter Ella at his introductory press conference on Aug. 11, 2026, in the Service Credit Union Victory Club. (Photo Credit: Alex Miller/UNH Athletics) “My daughter has fallen in love with volleyball,” Colton said. “This is really a family endeavor for me; my family is completely immersed in Wildcat athletics now.”

title: UNH leading effort to strengthen U.S. seafood supply through aquaculture - NBC Boston
content: Roughly 80% of the seafood Americans eat is imported, but a University of New Hampshire-led initiative is aiming to boost U.S. aquaculture — the farming of fish. Do you know where your seafood comes from? According to NOAA, roughly 80% of the seafood Americans eat is imported. Researchers at the University of New Hampshire are leading a major new effort aimed at growing more seafood domestically through sustainable aquaculture. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. Just a quarter mile off the coast of New Castle, UNH researchers are raising steelhead trout in a floating sea farm known as an Aquafort. It’s become a model for studying ways to make seafood production more sustainable. “We are growing fish at a very small community scale for the purpose of supplementing the seafood markets within the local area. So, the difference between wild-caught fish and aquaculture fish are hatched from eggs Our fish are actually hatched at a local New Hampshire hatchery up in Ossipee,” said David Fredriksson, director of UNH’s Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems. About 4,000 steelhead trout are taken to the floating pen, where they're raised for several months before harvest. The fish share the pen with sugar kelp and mussels. Researchers say those species act as natural biofilters, helping recycle nutrients and maintain balance within the ecosystem. The approach, known as integrated multi-trophic aquaculture, is designed to make seafood farming more environmentally sustainable by raising multiple species together. Fredriksson said his interest in aquaculture stems from a desire to build a more resilient domestic seafood supply. “I firmly believe that we need to make a change and we need to make a change with data, with science,” said Frederiksson. "We feel that with the data approach, we can do this in such a responsible way where we can reduce the effects of imported seafood coming into our markets." The goal, he said, is not to compete with local fishermen but to provide additional products to local seafood markets. "The only thing that we're competing with is imported salmon, which is a good product, but it's imported " Fredriksson said. "Can we do that at home with our own people? That's what I'm passionate about." Researchers hope to replicate similar small-scale sea farms in coastal communities around the country, tailoring each operation to local environmental and economic conditions. That effort recently received a major boost. UNH was selected to lead a new NOAA-supported initiative focused on strengthening America's seafood supply through aquaculture research. The NOAA Cooperative Institute Fostering Aquaculture Research and Markets (CIFARM) brings together research institutions from across the country to study ways to expand domestic seafood production. “The CIFARM is taking this type of model and adapting it to go to these other regions in the United States and start out small,” said Michael Chambers, research professor, Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems at University of New Hampshire. “Since this is a national effort, we want to cover all the exclusive economic zone waters of the United States. So, for example the UNH, their tentacles reach out into the Pacific Ocean to other islands such as American Samoa, Guam, Saipan, all the way down to University of Miami, their tentacles reach to the Caribbean, so USVI, and Puerto Rico, the Gulf and the West Coast and the Northeast so we have this expansive realm of experts to mobilize and expedite aquaculture in the US quickly. We’re just getting going now. We have a lot of work to do.” Locally, Chambers says the Aquafort provides an educational opportunity. “We bring people out on a weekly basis to look at what we do and not be afraid of what we do. As we build out these other farms we hope to do the same thing.” He said it's an opportunity to discuss the environmental impact of imported fish. “I would much rather eat fish from my backyard than bringing it from halfway across the world. Imagine the carbon footprint on that product that’s coming on in.” At the New Hampshire site, the team raises and distributes about 20,000 pounds of steelhead trout annually to local businesses, including Richard Pettigrew's seafood market in Portsmouth, Seaport Fish. "Having a local product right here that we can get pretty much on demand when they're harvesting to add to our product list is huge," Pettigrew said. He says consumers love buying a fish with a local backstory. “It’s just a New Hampshire-raised fish the whole way through,” said Pettigrew. "When you're buying aquaculture product, you can definitely tell if there's been love put into it.” Some of that locally raised trout also finds its way to community organizations, including Gather Food Pantry. The fish is smoked and packaged ready to eat. “By being able to offer something like the trout, we feel that just feeds into our mission of providing like food equity and dignity,” said Tania Marino, Deputy Director of Gather Food Pantry. “We have a lot of demand from our local unhoused population who don't have access to any cooking facilities. So for them to be able to come in and grab one of these pouches of this trout that's not only delicious and very nutritious, but something that they can just take and eat directly from the pouch is really valuable for them. Our older adults who are unable to cook for themselves anymore, they love it so much.” For pantry leaders, the partnership provides access to nutritious local food that might otherwise be out of reach. "It's very meaningful for us to be able to provide food," said Marino. "When we're able to say, 'Take home some steelhead trout,' it's not just a pouch of fish. It's a pouch of goodness and nutrition and love." Researchers hope efforts like these can demonstrate how aquaculture can support local economies, improve food access, and help strengthen the nation's seafood supply for years to come. title: UNH Jackson Estuarine Lab Expansion Opens in Durham, NH - Hoodline
content: The University of New Hampshire cut the ribbon this week on a $5.2 million expansion of its Jackson Estuarine Laboratory, a research outpost on Great Bay that has been studying New Hampshire's coastal waters since 1970. The new 4,500-square-foot addition brings dive lockers, boat storage and a dedicated meeting space to a facility perched on Adams Point, about five miles from UNH's Durham campus. UNH held the ribbon-cutting ceremony at the laboratory on Great Bay, according to the New Hampshire Union Leader. U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen joined UNH and state leaders at the event, the paper reports, marking a milestone for a lab that was among the nation's first academic facilities dedicated solely to studying estuaries. Great Bay itself is sometimes referred to as New Hampshire's hidden coastline, and the lab also studies the Hampton-Seabrook estuary further south. Shaheen called the laboratory's work “indispensable to advancing research on coastal ecosystems in New Hampshire and around the world,” per the Union Leader's reporting, and said the upgraded facility will support breakthroughs in building resiliency in estuarine and coastal systems. The senator helped secure more than $3 million in federal funding for the project, though a separate 2023 announcement from her office described $3.8 million heading to UNH to launch what it called a state-of-the-art water quality lab — the two figures were not reconciled in the available record. The addition includes a dedicated space for community partners and collaborators, a 36-person meeting room with an adjacent office, and a new entryway, according to the Union Leader. It also adds two high bays for working on vessels, buoys, and aquaculture and remote-sensing equipment, plus dive lockers with showers and room to store and repair scuba gear. The station already keeps three 19-foot outboard-powered center console boats on hand for fieldwork, per the UNH School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering, and the building and its adjoining greenhouse run on full seawater capability year-round. Erik Chapman, director of UNH's School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering and N.H. Sea Grant, said the project modernizes and expands the nearly 60-year-old laboratory and increases UNH's capacity for research, teaching and public service, the Union Leader reports. The Turner Group handled architecture and engineering for the project at an estimated cost of $5.2 million, while Tighe & Bond provided civil engineering and Milestone Construction took part in building the addition. The National Institute of Standards and Technology funded the expansion, with UNH contributing additional funding, and a second phase of renovations to the original building is still planned. The laboratory will serve as the permanent home of the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership and is set to host community collaborators including N.H. Fish and Game, the N.H. Department of Environmental Services, The Nature Conservancy N.H., and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems, according to the Union Leader. UNH also plans to provide a new minivan to improve collaborator and student access to the site across disciplines. That collaborative footprint matters because the bay itself is under strain. Eelgrass acreage in the Great Bay Estuary has faced decades of decline and took a significant drop in 2025, according to the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership. In response, PREP this year launched Great Bay's first seed-based eelgrass restoration effort, holding reproductive shoots in flowing seawater tanks at the Jackson lab. PREP and its partners collect more than 1 million data points annually to gauge the estuary's health. Water-quality data gathered through the lab's network show just how variable conditions in the bay have become. The Great Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve found that heavy winter precipitation lowered spring salinity in 2024, while a prolonged summer and fall drought pushed the estuary into high-salinity conditions, with measurements peaking at 31 parts per thousand in October of that year. Nutrient concentrations followed a similarly erratic pattern, running high through spring before hitting historic lows in summer and late fall, the reserve reported. The reserve's monitoring program is designed to track those kinds of shifts, identify new threats and measure whether management efforts are working. Its staff monitors saltmarsh health annually and works with partners to track mudflats, eelgrass and oyster beds — part of a System-Wide Monitoring Program that all 30 National Estuarine Research Reserves nationwide use to collect comparable data. The reserve also operates four water-quality stations and a weather station in coordination with the Jackson lab, while PREP sponsors additional monitoring stations, a coastal watershed data portal and a periodic State of Our Estuaries Report. UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said marine science and sustainability are longstanding strengths at the university and that UNH is committed to expanding its impact, according to the Union Leader's account of the ceremony. Chilton added that the expansion creates opportunities for students to work directly alongside scientists and gain hands-on experience. Research and monitoring tied to the laboratory focuses on water quality, environmental toxins, habitat restoration and aquaculture, and UNH frames that work as delivering economic and quality-of-life benefits for Granite Staters. The lab's reach extends well beyond New Hampshire's coastline. Estuaries, where rivers meet the ocean in partially enclosed brackish water, serve as sheltered spawning and feeding grounds that support nearly 70 percent of the nation's commercial fish catch, per UNH's marine science school. They also absorb floodwater and blunt the force of storms to protect property. Federal agencies including the EPA, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Army Corps of Engineers, USGS and NOAA all rely on the Jackson lab in their coastal resilience work, and local collaborators range from individual coastal towns to regional planning offices and groups like the Conservation Law Foundation and The Nature Conservancy. Over more than five decades, research tied to the laboratory has covered oysters, lobsters, horseshoe crabs and eelgrass, deepening understanding of coastal ecosystems, environmental quality and the links between watersheds and human health, according to UNH's marine science program. The facility also facilitates investment supporting New Hampshire's emerging aquaculture industry. With the new high bays, dive lockers and meeting space now in place, UNH officials say the Durham lab is positioned to keep expanding that body of work on a changing bay. title: Why Some Plants Grow Where Others Cannot - University of New Hampshire
content: Alders can thrive in soils that are inhospitable to other plants. Whether due to environmental changes, human-initiated uses, or some combination, the capacity for New Hampshire’s lands to sustain plant life is continually evolving. New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Stations scientists at the University of New Hampshire are discovering new ways that land with harsh, inhospitable soils and environments across the Granite State could be stewarded toward healthier, more productive conditions that support the state’s forests, natural resources, and food systems. The key has been understanding the relationship between microbes and fungal communities in soils near “pioneer” plants, which are able to grow where other plants simply cannot. Anyone who has battled weeds encroaching on driveways or patios knows that certain plants find a way to grow in unexpected places. Sometimes, however, environmental disruptions can be too harsh for just about any plant, such as in old landfills, strip mine or gravel pit sites, and areas where soil is salty or has been eroded. That’s where actinorhizal plants—plants including alders as well as bayberry, sweetfern, avens, and others that partner with nitrogen-fixing bacteria—gain a competitive advantage. For example, after Mount St. Helens erupted the first plants to repopulate the devastated countryside were actinorhizal, providing the natural first step toward restoration. “It’s imperative to understand how the pioneer plants’ microbiomes change over time at different locations and in relation to environmental disturbances and contaminants,” says Station scientist Louis S. Tisa, professor of microbiology and genetics in the department of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences. “That knowledge will provide the foundation for successful and lasting partner-planting and bioremediation efforts at ecologically damaged sites like landfills, or even the 22 superfund sites in New Hampshire.” Pioneer plants such as alders (Alnus rugosa) often play vital roles in land reclamation projects. To better understand why, Tisa and Alexandra Gomez ’G27, a doctoral candidate in microbiology in the UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, studied microbial characteristics in bacterial and fungal communities within alder root nodules, immediately next to the roots, and in the surrounding soil across six different New Hampshire sites during every season of a three-year research period. In a paper chosen as an Editor’s Pick in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Gomez and Tisa showed that the root nodule and soil microbiomes vary in different locations—from pristine rural freshwater wetland site to those located near major roadways and subject to vehicular exhaust and contaminant runoff—underscoring the importance of understanding environmental and soil variables for land reclamation. While not as inhospitable as some environments, New Hampshire roadside soils are exposed to salt, metals, water-soluble chemicals from asphalt, exhaust byproducts, and other contaminants. Of the six sites studied, five were near roadways but differing in other respects. The sixth site, in Candia, was rural, near to freshwater peatlands and far from any roadways. In addition to proximity to a roadway, the Hampton site was next to a saltwater marsh, the Durham site was close to a freshwater wetland, the Epping site was urban, the Durham-adjacent site was wooded, and the Raymond site was near a highway but not water. “Alex did a really good field study and picked the locations well,” says Tisa. “We were able to see interesting differences in the microbial populations among the sites, reflecting the different environmental conditions and seasonal variability.” The study’s findings show that the microbial populations in and around the alder root nodules were different from site to site, and they also showed seasonal variation. The Candia site had the lowest overall bacterial diversity, perhaps because the high levels of aluminum and sulfur in the soil, typical for peatlands, selected for certain species. The nitrogen-fixing bacterium Frankia also dominated the bacterial populations within the Candia alders’ root nodules. At the roadside sites, high levels of soil zinc strongly shaped the microbial communities. The relative amount of Frankia varied between the roadside sites, with the Epping and Hampton sites having the highest relative nodule occupancy. Another important factor shaping the microbial populations was soil moisture, as the three sites with the most Frankia had more consistent water sources than the Raymond and Durham sites. Drought also played a role in one of the years. Typically, Frankia relative abundance peaks with high summer photosynthesis rates, but a spring and summer drought in 2022 pushed peak abundance from July to October region-wide. Nitrogen fixation within the root nodules and alder viability may therefore be limited in areas with insufficient soil moisture. title: UNH to hold memorial for hockey player killed in wrong way crash - WFSB
content:
WEST HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - A hockey player police said was killed in a wrong way crash was remembered by the university for which he played. Ryan O’Shea, 21, was hit by the wrong way driver on I-91 south in North Haven on Oct. 16, according to police. The driver, 31-year-old Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, remains in the hospital. The University of New Haven said he was returning to its campus following a game. His legacy was honored at a ceremony, which ended with a plaque in his honor being unveiled. It bears his name in the heart of the campus. “It was really just heartbreaking to see someone so innocent like that just lose a life in such a horrible way,” said Aidan Dowsett, a UNH alum and friend of O’Shea. He described O’Shea as selfless and positive. They stayed close despite only spending a year on campus together. “It really just shows what type of person he was. Even at 21 years old how many people you could touch it’s truly amazing,” he added. “He kind of fit the ethos of the university of New Haven which is ‘Care for the human good.’ He really put himself, you know, behind and put others first,” said Devon Crosby, Director of Athletics, University of New Haven. A scholarship fund will help others follow in O’Shea’s footsteps. To date, more than $55,000 has been raised. “We’ll always be saying Ryan’s name for years to come,” added Crosby. “…obviously nothing amounts to him actually being here, but we’re going to try our best as alumni as a community to remember him as much as we can," said Dowsett. The hockey team plays its first home game since O’Shea’s death Friday night at 8:00 p.m. against Wentworth. A full house is expected for the contest. title: UNH Marks Jackson Estuarine Laboratory Expansion at Ribbon-Cutting - University of New Hampshire
content: U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (with scissors) cuts the ribbon on UNH’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory expansion with School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering Director Erik Chapman (to her right), UNH President Elizabeth Chilton (to her left), Jackson Estuarine Laboratory Director David Burdick (to Chilton's left), and state and community partners. New Hampshire’s estuaries and coastal economies are about to get even healthier, thanks to a major expansion at UNH’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory on Great Bay. At a ribbon-cutting ceremony Oct. 26, 2026, U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen joined UNH and state leaders to celebrate the completion of the project, which added 4,500 square feet of enhanced facilities for studying estuaries. “The work done at the University of New Hampshire’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory has been indispensable in advancing critical research that allows us to better understand our coastal ecosystems in New Hampshire and around the world,” says Shaheen. “I was proud to help secure over $3 million in federal funding to improve the state-of-the-art lab and ensure it has the resources it needs to continue its groundbreaking work, and it was great to see the facility improvements behind this project earlier today. I know this upgraded facility will lead to new breakthroughs for building resiliency in our estuarine and coastal systems. I can’t wait to see all that lies ahead.” “Marine science and sustainability are longstanding strengths at UNH, and we're committed to building on that expertise to make an even greater impact in New Hampshire and beyond. This expansion represents an important investment in that work,” says UNH President Elizabeth Chilton. “Just as importantly, we're creating new opportunities for students to work alongside experienced scientists and gain hands-on experience addressing real-world challenges.” Visitors to Jackson Estuarine Laboratory tour the new facility, including its high bay. Among the features of the Jackson Estuarine Laboratory (JEL) expansion: Two high bays for working on vessels, buoys, and equipment for aquaculture and remote sensing; Dive lockers with showers and space for storage and repair of SCUBA equipment; “This project modernizes and expands UNH’s nearly 60-year-old laboratory on New Hampshire’s Great Bay, elevating UNH's capacity for estuarine research, teaching, and public service,” says Erik Chapman, director of UNH’s School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering and N.H. Sea Grant. “Research and monitoring focused on water quality, environmental toxins, habitat restoration, and aquaculture deliver direct economic and quality-of-life benefits for Granite Staters.” JEL will also serve as the permanent home of the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership and will host community partners and collaborators — including N.H. Fish and Game, N.H. Department of Environmental Services, The Nature Conservancy N.H., and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems (NERACOOS) — in dedicated space. A new minivan will increase access for collaborators and for UNH students in a range of disciplines. A second phase of the project will involve renovations and updates to the original building. Built in 1970 and located on Great Bay in Durham, five miles from the UNH campus, JEL was the one of the nation’s first academic labs dedicated solely to studying estuaries. Research at the lab helps understand, protect, and manage New Hampshire’s estuaries — Great Bay, sometimes called New Hampshire’s “hidden coastline,” and the Hampton-Seabrook estuary — and advances the state’s coastal economy. Research at JEL, spanning oysters, lobsters, horseshoe crabs, eelgrass, and more, has improved our understanding of coastal ecosystems, environmental quality, and the connection between watershed and human health. Estuaries, partially enclosed bodies of brackish water where rivers meet the ocean, are among the most productive habitats on Earth. They provide sheltered spawning and feeding grounds and are habitat for nearly 70 percent of the U.S. commercial fish catch, and they absorb flood water and mitigate the effects of storms to protect property. Total cost for the Jackson Estuarine Laboratory expansion is estimated to be $5.2 million. Funding for the project is from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), with additional funding from UNH. The Turner Group (Concord) were architects and engineers, Tighe & Bond (Portsmouth) provided civil engineering, and Milestone Construction (Concord) managed construction. As the largest enterprise in the managed-care group and a heavyweight across the broader medical economy, its claims experience serves as a barometer for how costs are trending across the American system. Peers, providers and market participants alike parse its quarterly commentary for signals about where medical spending is heading and how plans are adapting. For the period ahead, the task is to keep the margin improvement in place while medical use stays elevated and to keep the services arm growing as a steadying counterweight to the benefits base. title: Why Durham House of Pizza is still loved by UNH community after 50 years - Granite Post News
content: DHOP, as it’s affectionately known by local residents and University of New Hampshire students, is a cornerstone of the college town community. In November, the business that is still owned and operated by the same family will celebrate 50 years in business. The steaming slice, the checkerboard floor, the chef statue at the front door, the shelter of the black awning bearing its name, the wonderful smell that hits you the minute you get in the door. Decades of diners have enjoyed the food, the familiarity and the family of Durham House of Pizza. DHOP, as it’s affectionately known by local residents and University of New Hampshire students, is a cornerstone of the college town community. In November, the business that is still owned and operated by the same family will celebrate 50 years in business. To keep reading—and get local New Hampshire news sent daily to your inbox—sign up for our free newsletter! The Petrovitsis family’s commitment to serving consistently great pizzas, calzones and salads is eclipsed only by its commitment to the community. For five decades, the business has donated to local and student organizations and nonprofits, employed a legion of students and local residents, created a place for families and friends to gather, catered special celebrations, supported local teams and events, and quietly served anyone in need. When Stephen Petrovitsis and his father, James, opened the restaurant in November 1976, Stephen was living in Peabody, Massachusetts, where he grew up, and commuting to Durham seven days a week around his 18-hour restaurant shifts. Stephen had been working in a friend’s sandwich shop, his father wanted to set him up in business, and they decided on a pizza restaurant. It was first located in what is now the Mill Pond Plaza, where most recently the Rite Aid pharmacy was located. Stephen was 19 years old. They used family recipes for the pizza dough and sauce. His father made a special Greek salad dressing. A small pizza cost $1.35. A large pizza rang in at $2.50. Stephen’s father was in real estate and owned several buildings in town over the years, and in 1982 the restaurant moved into the building behind where it’s now located at 38 Main St. Stephen Petrovitsis continued to work very hard building the business along with members of his family and students they hired. He lived in apartments in his family’s buildings, which meant it was easier to do those long hours the restaurant required. He married his wife, Rennie, in 1987, and the newlyweds bought a home in Madbury. Rennie was a nurse, but joined the family business and played a huge part in it. They had four sons — James, Justin, Jordan and John — and raised them attending Oyster River schools, but they might have spent more time at the restaurant than at home. The boys often joke they went “from crib to crust.” “I remember being on tiptoe, stretching to reach the counter and trying to help serve slices,” Jordan said. They were surrounded by aunts, uncles, cousins and other family members who helped behind the counter. Eventually, in 1991, the couple opened JP’s Grill, the restaurant next door, named it for their sons, and their mom Rennie managed JP’s while their dad managed DHOP. They sold JP’s about two years ago, and now Justin, Jordan and John manage DHOP as their dad tries to step away from the business, even though he admits he still stops in most days. “It’s kind of exciting. So many things have changed over the years,” Stephen said of the 50th anniversary. “I’m very proud.” Durham House of Pizza moves to a new generation in family The checkerboard floor is gone. A recent renovation replaced it and put in marble countertops. The dining room is the same with updated decor and seats 48. Petro, the pizza chef statue, is still at the door. Kids still stop and beg their parents to take photos with him. Stephen’s parents’ photos are still in a corner as they’ve always been, next to a poster celebrating DHOP’s 40th anniversary. “Mom and Dad are over there watching us all the time,” Stephen said. “They keep an eye on us.” Stephen said he used to run a promotion asking customers to take a photo of a DHOP T-shirt wherever they were in the world and send it to him to display; one came back to him from Egypt. The T-shirts now read “Live Free and Eat Pizza” and “Hot Girls Eat Pizza” and can be bought online. They’ve started bottling Papou’s Famous Greek Dressing, a recipe developed by Stephen’s father James that they use on the DHOP Greek salad, and selling it online and at the restaurant. The restaurant just started selling beer, including local brews like Stoneface Brewing’s Sunday Sauce, of course, and Deciduous Brewing’s Go ‘Cats. “The best thing I ever did was transfer the business over to these kids because they do a great job. I’m very proud of them,” Stephen said. Since 2012, the three brothers started joining the business as they graduated from school. “You can never complain about learning from somebody that’s done this their whole life, 50 years,” Justin said about working with his father. “It’s a lot of knowledge to absorb and you learn a work ethic. You learn how to respect the customers and appreciate everything, and just enjoy your job.” They said they learned living in and growing up in the restaurant environment. Only one studied and earned a degree in restaurant management. “We all work really well together. No drama involved. We all kind of understand,” Justin said. “We’re here to do the same thing, and we’ve all been taught by him to do the exact same things.” Jordan said he appreciates “working together and staying close with everyone in the family. I like working in a family small business.” That family business, which usually employs between 15 and 20, attracts and retains employees, who become family themselves. “I think that’s why our employees enjoy working with us so much. It’s a much closer feel. We see our employees years and years later,” John said, noting he met up with a former manager at a restaurant in the Netherlands, where he lives now, for a visit. “It’s a very different feel from working in a corporate-owned kitchen,” Justin said. DHOP changes with times, but favorites and traditions remain They said their best-selling items are still cheese and pepperoni pizzas as Nos. 1 and 2. Of their specialty pizzas, they said it’s The Mediterranean with spinach, artichoke hearts, feta cheese and tomatoes. The Greek salad is popular, too. Stephen’s favorite pizza is cheese “plain and simple.” Justin’s favorite on the menu is the cheesy breadsticks, followed by the chicken club pizza with chicken and bacon. John’s favorite is the cheese pizza “because if you can make a great cheese pizza, you can put any toppings on it and it will be great.” Jordan’s favorite is pepperoni with “an unhealthy handful of fresh red pepper” on it. DHOP serves between 1,000 to 2,000 pizzas a week on average, depending on the week and what’s happening on campus. If there’s a sports game, especially a UNH hockey game, or the recent Parents Weekend, they know it’s going to be busy, really busy. On a busy day, they said, they can go through 1,000 pounds of cheese and make 1,200 to 1,500 pizzas. Their busiest day of the year has become Kentucky Derby Day, they said. It used to be Cinco de Mayo, but because that moves around a lot and can happen on a Monday, for example, they said since the pandemic, the students are making a much bigger deal of the Kentucky Derby. It’s always on the first Saturday in May so they know they don’t have school, it’s getting nice outside, it’s toward the end of the semester, and they all like getting dressed up for parties. They said DHOP can serve 2,000 pizzas on that one day, with a line out the door from 1 p.m. to 2 a.m. They said they get it all done with planning, organization, “science,” and loving it. “We all kind of thrive on the chaos,” John said. “I like the stress.” One of the reasons for DHOP’s longevity is the family’s decision to “always be fair,” as Stephen puts it. It’s a place you can feed the family affordably, or a starving student can always afford to grab a slice. “We did the $1.50 slice as our late-night special for years,” Justin said, serving as the place students could grab something hot late at night when the bars were closing. UNH alumni fondly remember DHOP daily specials that made for appointment dining for their group of friends. Families of the 1990s remember looking forward weekly to the Tuesday Two (large cheese pizzas) for $10 special. “Monday night, she’s pretty popular,” Stephen said of the current 2026 Monday special of a small cheese pizza for $7.95. If it’s Tuesday, it’s $11.50 for a large 16-inch pizza. If it’s Wednesday, the special is a super 20-inch cheese pizza for $19.50. Thursdays bring a cheese calzone for $7.50, just to name a few. Monday through Friday, the lunch special is two slices and a soda for $9. “We’ve met so many, so many good customers. … from Lee, Madbury, of course, Durham, the students at UNH, faculty, staff. We have so much to be thankful for,” Stephen said. “I’ve met kids from all over the country. Politicians, they all come into the store. That’s the biggest thing that I like about being in business is meeting the people.” “Being on a college campus, it’s like every four years, it’s a new batch of people,” Justin said. “We have four years of new people to meet, and the town is such a small local community. We do our best to focus on the Durham community while also being on a college campus, supporting the locals, and it’s interesting to see how the town has changed over the years.” “It’s a constant cycle of new people all the time. It’s good to meet the new locals, meet the new students, and build a community of people you know,” Justin said. “We get so many regulars in here. It’s like you become friends with them at the same time so it’s fun.” Durham House of Pizza‘s connections run deep in UNH, Durham community Of the restaurant’s success, Stephen said, “It’s really not the pizza, it’s the people.” He thinks of the people who once worked at DHOP and bring their own kids to college at UNH and return for a meal. He remembers the people who met there and ended up getting married. He said former employees will come in and ask if they can work while they’re in town visiting. Stephen has stayed in touch with at least one of his employees from back in 1976. He remembers all the UNH athletes who became regulars at the restaurant, especially hockey players who went on to become professional athletes, and who he’s followed through the years. He was once traveling in Greece and heard someone say, “Hey, there’s the DHOP guy.” “I give as much as I can,” Stephen said about his community involvement. He remembers the tough time during the COVID pandemic shutdown when the students were all gone and they were only taking pizzas out to the curb to people in their cars. He said he received so many notes and letters from customers thanking the family, some containing $50 or $100 checks. “I couldn’t believe what I was getting in the mail,” he said. “That touched me so much. I was opening them and saying, ‘Are you kidding me?’ It was the thought and what they wrote. It was unbelievable they would do that. This community backed us so much, and I can’t thank them enough. When I see them, it’s not a hello, it’s a hug.” He said it’s important to him for his business to give back. “My father always said one hand shakes the other. You have to help. You can’t just take. You got to give. So I give as much as I can,” Stephen said. “My dad always said, if someone comes through that door and if they don’t have any money, you give them anything they want. … If someone needs something, I’m there for them. And that’s what I passed on to the boys, and they think the same.” This article originally appeared on Fosters Daily Democrat.  has spent much of the past year rebuilding investor confidence after a difficult stretch of rising medical costs and lower profitability. Its third-quarter report marked another step in that recovery. Profit rose sharply, the company beat analyst forecasts and full-year guidance moved higher again. Revenue was slightly lower than a year ago, but that was largely by design, as the company shed less profitable members. Healthcare stocks across the NYSE Composite have been sensitive to policy headlines and cost trends, so a clean margin improvement from the largest U.S. health insurer drew close attention. Consolidated revenue was roughly flat compared with the prior year, while earnings from operations rose substantially. Adjusted earnings per share came in well ahead of the consensus estimate. Cash flow from operations was healthy and exceeded net income, a sign of solid earnings quality. The company described the quarter as a period of discipline and execution, focused on making its businesses simpler and more supportive for patients and clinicians. In practical terms, that meant tighter pricing, adjusted benefit designs and better coordination of care. The medical care ratio shows how much of each premium dollar is spent on patient care. When it rises, profit margins shrink. UnitedHealth's ratio improved meaningfully from the prior year, helped by medical cost management, pricing discipline and benefit design changes. Part of the improvement came from favorable development in reserves set aside for earlier periods of the year. Analysts noted that this reserve release flattered the headline ratio, so the underlying improvement is somewhat smaller. Even so, the direction of travel was clearly positive. The operating cost ratio declined compared with last year, reflecting investments to modernize operations and streamline administrative processes. Lower overhead relative to revenue gives the company more room to absorb cost swings. Optum, the company's health services arm, played a major role in the quarter. Optum Health, which provides care through physician networks and value-based arrangements, swung from barely profitable a year ago to a meaningful profit contributor. Management credited operational discipline and better medical cost management in value-based care markets. This turnaround is important because Optum is central to UnitedHealth's long-term strategy of combining insurance with care delivery, pharmacy services and data analytics. UnitedHealthcare served fewer members than a year earlier across Medicare, Medicaid and employer plans. Some of this was intentional, as the company repriced plans and stepped back from less profitable business. Employer attrition also contributed. Management indicated that commercial cost trends are running above its initial assumptions, driven by specialty drugs, higher clinician costs and arbitration under federal billing rules, though the trend appears to be stabilizing. UnitedHealth raised its full-year outlook for both reported and adjusted earnings per share, expressed as a minimum level rather than a range. That wording leaves room for fourth-quarter cost swings while signaling confidence. It was the third time this year the company lifted its outlook. Investors are now looking ahead to a fuller view of next year, which the company is expected to share before year-end. Key items include pricing, benefit design and progress on reducing prior authorization requirements, a commitment aimed at easing administrative burden for patients and providers. Several uncertainties remain. Commercial medical costs may stay elevated. Government reimbursement levels, Medicare Advantage rules and quality star ratings can shift profitability. The company also faces an ongoing federal investigation and continued scrutiny of its pharmacy benefit practices, including a commitment to pass through manufacturer rebates in coming years. Beyond the numbers, UnitedHealth is reshaping how it operates. The company has committed to reducing the number of services that require prior authorization, a process that patients and doctors have long criticized for delays and paperwork. Simplifying these steps is intended to improve the experience for patients and clinicians while lowering administrative costs. Technology plays a growing role as well. Investments in automation, data analytics and modernized claims systems are designed to make the business more efficient and more accurate. The improvement in the operating cost ratio suggests these efforts are beginning to show results. Leadership has also emphasized affordability. By aligning benefits and pricing more closely with actual costs, the company aims to keep premiums sustainable for employers and government programs. Balancing affordability with profitability will remain a central challenge, but the latest quarter indicates that the company has regained some control over that balance. Watchers of Healthcare Stocks often view UnitedHealth as a bellwether for managed care. A recovering margin profile suggests that insurers are adapting to higher utilization through pricing and plan changes. If the improvement proves durable, it may ease some of the pressure that has weighed on the group. This was a margin-recovery quarter rather than a growth quarter. The next test is whether UnitedHealth can grow earnings while membership stays flat or declines. Upcoming guidance for next year will provide the clearest answer and will likely set the tone for the stock in the months ahead.
